'''Tudor Ganea''' (October 17, 1922 &ndash;August 1971)<ref>[https://www.ancientfaces.com/person/tudor-ganea/37120331 Biographical information]</ref> was a [[Romanian Americans|Romanian-American]] mathematician, known for his work in [[algebraic topology]], especially [[homotopy]] theory. Ganea left [[Socialist Republic of Romania|Communist Romania]] to settle in the [[United States]] in the early 1960s.<ref name="Revista 22">{{cite web|url=https://revista22.ro/bucurestiul-cultural/bucurestiul-cultural-nr-72006|first=Alexandru|last=Cistelecan
|title=Iritarea la români|series=Bucureștiul Cultural, nr. 7/2006| date=May 26, 2006|publisher=[[Revista 22]]| language=Romanian|accessdate=May 3, 2020}}</ref> He taught at the [[University of Washington]].

== Life and work==
He studied mathematics at the [[University of Bucharest]], and then started his research as a member of [[Simion Stoilow]]'s seminar on complex functions. His  papers from 1949–1952 were on [[covering space]]s, [[topological group]]s, [[Symmetric product (topology)|symmetric products]], and the [[Lusternik–Schnirelmann category]]. During this time, he earned his candidate thesis in topology under the direction of Stoilow.<ref name="tproc">{{citation|title=Topology in Eastern Europe 1900–1950|first=Sibe|last=Mardešić|author-link=Sibe Mardešić|journal=Topology Proceedings|volume= 25 |year=2000|issue=Spring|pages=397–430|url=http://topology.nipissingu.ca/tp/reprints/v25/tp25127.pdf|mr=1875605}}</ref>

In 1957, Ganea published in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' a short, yet influential paper with [[Samuel Eilenberg]], in which the [[Eilenberg–Ganea theorem]] was proved and the celebrated [[Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture]] was formulated. The conjecture is still open.

By 1958, Ganea and his mentee, {{ill|Israel Berstein|ro}}, were the two leading algebraic topologists in Romania.<ref>[https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/19108/Berstein_Israel_1991.pdf Israel Berstein, June 23, 1926—September 22, 1991]</ref> Later that year at an international conference on geometry and topology in [[Iași]], the two met [[Peter Hilton]], starting long mathematical collaborations. Ganea left for France in 1961, where he obtained in 1962 his Ph.D. from the [[University of Paris]] under [[Henri Cartan]],<ref name="tproc"/> with thesis ''Sur quelques invariants numeriques du type d'homotopie''.<ref>{{citation|first=Tudor|last=Ganea|title=Sur quelques invariants numeriques du type d'homotopie|language=fr|publisher=Faculté des sciences de Paris|year=1962|location=Paris, France|oclc=1672078}}</ref> He then emigrated to the United States. After spending a year at [[Purdue University]] in [[West Lafayette, Indiana]], he joined the faculty at the [[University of Washington]] in [[Seattle]].<ref name="tproc"/>

During this time, he tried to get [[Aurora Cornu]] (his fiancée at the time) out of Romania, but did not succeed.<ref name="Revista 22" /> In 1962, he gave an invited talk at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Stockholm]], titled ''On some numerical homotopy invariants.''

Just before he died, Ganea attended the Symposium on Algebraic Topology, held February 22–26, 1971 at the Battelle Seattle Research Center, in Seattle.<ref>{{cite book|title=Symposium on Algebraic Topology. Battelle Seattle Research Center, Seattle, Wash., 22–26 February 1971. Dedicated to the memory of Tudor Ganea (1922–1971)|editor-first= Peter J. |editor-last=Hilton|editor-link=Peter Hilton|series= [[Lecture Notes in Mathematics]]|volume= 249|publisher= [[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer-Verlag]]|location= Berlin-New York|year=1971|mr=0328907| url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/bfm%3A978-3-540-37082-6%2F1.pdf|doi=10.1007/BFb0060889|isbn=978-3-540-05715-4 }}</ref> At the symposium, he was not able to give a talk, but he did distribute a preprint containing a list of unsolved problems. One of these problems, regarding the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category, came to be known as ''[[Ganea conjecture|Ganea's conjecture]]''. A version of this conjecture for rational spaces was proved by [[Kathryn Hess]] in her 1989 [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] Ph.D. thesis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hess|first=Kathryn P.|authorlink=Kathryn Hess|title=A proof of Ganea's conjecture for rational spaces|journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]]|language=en|volume=30|issue=2|pages=205–214|doi=10.1016/0040-9383(91)90006-p|year=1991|mr=1098914|doi-access=free}}</ref> Many particular cases of Ganea's original conjecture were proved, until [[Norio Iwase]] provided a counterexample in 1998.<ref>{{Cite journal |first=Norio|last=Iwase| title=Ganea's conjecture on Lusternik–Schnirelmann category|journal=[[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]]|volume= 30 |year=1998|issue=6|pages=623–634|doi=10.1112/S0024609398004548|mr=1642747|citeseerx=10.1.1.509.2343|s2cid=6881044 }}</ref> A minimum dimensional counterexample to Ganea’s conjecture was constructed by Don Stanley and Hugo Rodríguez Ordóñez in 2010.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stanley|first1=Donald|last2=Rodríguez Ordóñez|first2=Hugo|year=2010|title=A minimum dimensional counterexample to Ganea's conjecture|journal=[[Topology and Its Applications]]|volume=157|issue=14| pages=2304–2315|doi=10.1016/j.topol.2010.06.009|mr=2670507|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Ganea is buried at [[Lake View Cemetery (Seattle)|Lake View Cemetery]] in Seattle.
